A1.justification: Both PDFs describe NanoQuant and contain readable text, equations, figures, tables and appendices. Matching the retained, relocated and revised material supports a reliable comparison.

before.justification: Section 4 and Appendices D-E report original quantization results, component ablations, and measurements of inference throughput, memory and energy.

after.justification: Original empirical results are retained, with additional calibration-dataset experiments, ADMM ablations, GemLite comparisons and generated text examples.

M1.justification: The low-rank binary representation, Hessian-aware ADMM initialization, magnitude balancing, block refinement and scale-only model reconstruction remain unchanged. Algorithm 1 becomes more explicit, but the revisions do not establish a different underlying procedure.

E1.justification: Appendix D.2 adds C4 for calibration and perplexity evaluation alongside WikiText-2 on Qwen3-4B and Llama-2-7B. This expands the data distributions tested within existing language-modeling coverage; the commonsense benchmarks are retained.

E2.justification: Appendix E.4 adds GemLite binary kernels as an evaluated comparison backend on H100 and A100 GPUs. AQLM, AQLM with PV-Tuning and QTIP were already evaluated in v1's appendix, and the principal binary PTQ and QAT comparator families remain.

E3.justification: Table 8 replaces the earlier vector-quantization variant comparison with comparisons organized around 1-, 1.5- and 2-bit targets. Figure 6 changes GPTQ from 2-bit/group-64 to 2- and 3-bit/group-128 and revises NanoQuant's displayed bit configurations. New protocols vary C4/WikiText-2 composition at a fixed 128 samples and test 100-1600 ADMM iterations and three penalty schedules on Gemma-4-31B block 0.

E4.justification: New analyses test calibration-source sensitivity (Table 10), ADMM iteration and scheduling choices (Figure 9), kernel backend performance (Figures 12-13), and qualitative generation at three bit widths (Table 15). These substantially extend the questions examined; the existing component, data-budget and latent-weight analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions disclose seed 0 for calibration-data selection in Appendix C. Neither introduces repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals or significance testing; the added experiments continue reporting point estimates and individual trajectories.

E6.justification: Table 2 changes NanoQuant's Gemma-3-27B perplexities at 1.00/0.80/0.55 bits from 32.98/32.84/45.59 to 27.21/28.83/32.98. Table 8 and Figure 6 revise results under changed comparison settings, while the calibration, ADMM, GemLite and generation analyses add substantial results. The reported RTX 3050 speedup changes from 4.02x to 3.7x, and Appendix F removes the Llama-3-405B storage and BPW estimates.

T1.justification: Appendices A, B and F retain the same mathematical arguments, assumptions, proofs and storage formulas. Appendix B is retitled from 'Convergence Analysis' to 'Stability Analysis'; the main-text notation changes clarify existing objectives without adding or revising theoretical results.

C1.justification: The abstract drops the claim of state-of-the-art accuracy at sub-1-bit compression, while the introduction and Figure 1 emphasize competitive accuracy at lower effective storage. The central sub-1-bit PTQ, Pareto-frontier and large-model deployment contributions remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations linking calibration diversity to reduced overfitting and ADMM settings to optimization-cost versus reconstruction-quality tradeoffs. The limitations qualify superiority to 'some' 2-bit baselines and add adaptive layerwise rank allocation as future work.

D1.justification: v2 explicitly identifies the five tasks averaged in Table 8 and supplies the shared generation prompt in Appendix G. The new ablations document sample mixtures, iteration budgets, schedules and the tested block. Appendix C's original learning rates, training durations, software versions and hardware specifications remain unchanged.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds substantial positioning within classical and nonconvex ADMM research and its applications to quantization, factorization and sparsification. It also acknowledges QMoE and BTC-LLM as prior sub-1-bit approaches, while Section 3 explicitly relates the factorization to LittleBit and DBF. Publication-year and venue updates alone are not counted.

P1.justification: Most prose and the main section sequence are retained. Changes include localized language edits, clearer pseudocode, the revised Appendix B heading, acknowledgments, and moving the vector-quantization discussion from Appendix D.1 into Section 4.5.

P2.justification: Figure 6 is redrawn with revised series and legends, and Table 8 is rebuilt around bit-budget groups and explicit bit values. New calibration and generation tables and multi-panel ADMM and kernel figures substantially expand the visual presentation. Existing Figure 7 moves into the main text, and the storage-bound tables are placed together.

improvement.justification: v2 strengthens validation of the retained method through calibration-distribution tests, optimizer ablations and a relevant binary-kernel comparator. More restrained accuracy claims and expanded research positioning also improve clarity. These gains are limited by unresolved reporting inconsistencies: the new Table 10 reports WikiText-only Qwen3-4B perplexity of 21.25, whereas Table 2 reports 14.29, without explaining the difference.
